uosdwashi-dgenerationport-readme.text:
# D/Generation — a source port

A native rebuild of *D/Generation* (Robert Cook, Mindscape, 1991) for Linux and Windows,
written in C++23 with SDL3. The game was reverse engineered from its DOS program (the VGA
version, 1.0) and reimplemented to play exactly as the original does: the same rooms, the same
timing, the same sound and music on an emulated AdLib or the PC speaker, the same endings.

Around the game the port adds what a modern program should have: a main menu, settings
changed in the game, keys that can be rebound, saved games in slots, the picture scaled to
any window or the full screen at 4:3, smooth motion between the game's frames, and volume
levels for the music, the effects and the menu. None of it changes how the game plays.

**The game's files are not included.** The port needs a copy of the original D/Generation
(the DOS version 1.0, with its VGA graphics): its pictures, rooms, sounds and text are read
from that copy as the game starts.

## Playing

Download the package for your system from the releases and unpack it anywhere:

- **Linux** (x86-64, glibc 2.38 or later, 2023's distributions onwards):
  `dgen-1.0.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`
- **Windows** (10 and 11, 64-bit): `dgen-1.0.0-windows-x86_64.zip`

Then copy the original game's files into the `GameData` folder beside `dgen`: everything in
the folder `DGENVGA.EXE` is in, with its `DATA` and `VGA` folders (`GameData/README.txt` says
more). Start `dgen` (`dgen.exe` on Windows). If something is missing or damaged, it says which
files.

Everything the game writes stays in its folder: the settings in `dgen.ini`, made on the first
run, and the saved games in `Saves`. The folder can be moved or copied as a whole.

### Keys

These are the defaults; every one can be changed in Options › Controls or in `dgen.ini`.

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Arrows | Move straight |
| Keypad 7/9/1/3, Home/PgUp/End/PgDn, or two arrows | Move along the room's axes |
| Space | Fire the laser |
| T | Throw a grenade |
| U | Items (left/right pick, Return uses, Escape closes) |
| Return | Speak to the person in sight (arrows pick a question, Return asks) |
| S | Show the status |
| P, Pause | Pause |
| Escape | The main menu |
| F1 | Options |
| Alt+Return, F11 | Window or full screen |
| Ctrl+S | Sound off and on |
| Alt+S, Alt+R | Save the game as it was on reaching the floor, and restore it (as the original) |
| Ctrl+A, Ctrl+R | Restart the room with a life less; go back to the floor's start |
| Ctrl+Q | Quit |

### The menu

The main menu comes up on the title card: New Game, Load Game, Options, Help and Quit. In a
game, Escape brings it up over the waiting game, with Resume and Save Game. Games are saved in
eight slots besides the quick save of Alt+S; a save holds what the original's `SAVE.DAT` holds,
so a game loaded starts again at the start of its floor. Left alone at the menu for a minute,
the title's pictures and demos play.

Options has the display (full screen, 4:3 or square pixels, fitting the window or whole
multiples only, the filter, smooth motion), the sound's levels and the keys. Changes take effect
at once and are written to `dgen.ini`, which explains every setting and keeps your comments.

### The command line

```
dgen [<game-folder>] [--scene <n>] [--entry <slot>] [--armed] [--demo <n>] [--speaker]
     [--quiet] [--scale <n>] [--save <file>] [--config <file>]
     [--frames <n>] [--dump <folder>] [--wav <file>]
```

`<game-folder>` plays a copy of the game from elsewhere instead of `GameData`. `--scene` starts
in that room (`--entry` at one of its entry points, `--armed` with the laser and grenades),
`--demo` plays attract demo 0 or 1, `--speaker` plays the sound on the PC speaker instead of the
AdLib, and `--quiet` starts with the sound off, as the original's `-q`. `--frames` runs that
many frames as fast as they go and stops; with `--dump` it writes each frame as a picture and
with `--wav` the sound to a file, which together allow runs without a display
(`SDL_VIDEO_DRIVER=offscreen`).

## Building

Needs CMake 3.25 or later, a C++23 compiler (GCC 14 or later, or a recent Clang) and SDL 3.4
or later.

```sh
cmake --preset release
cmake --build --preset release
build/release/src/app/dgen <game-folder>
```

The release packages are made with `packaging/build-release.sh linux` and
`packaging/build-release.sh windows`, on Linux: the script builds SDL from its source release,
then the game against it (cross-compiled with MinGW-w64 for Windows), and packs the folder the
player unpacks. `cmake --install <build> --prefix <folder>` makes the same folder without
packing it.

| Path | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `src/data/` | Reading the original's files: palettes, pictures, sprite banks, rooms, the map, demos |
| `src/render/` | Drawing into 256-colour pictures: rooms' backgrounds |
| `src/game/` | The game: the room and every kind of thing in it (`entities/`), people and talk, terminals, the story, the status bar and the game's text |
| `src/audio/` | The sound: the AdLib driver reimplemented, the PC speaker, the OPL chip, the mixer |
| `src/assets/` | Finding and checking a copy of the game, and loading it |
| `src/app/` | The play session, the title and the demos, and `main` |
| `src/platform/` | The port's own layer: settings, controls, the menu, saved games, where things are kept |
| `src/shell/` | The SDL front end: the window, the sound device, the keys and the frame loop |
| `packaging/` | The release folder and packages, the MinGW toolchain |
| `third_party/` | Nuked OPL3 and the Modern DOS 8x8 font (below) |

## Licence

Copyright © 2026 Bloog.

The port is free software: you can redistribute it and change it under the terms of the GNU
General Public License, version 3 or (at your option) any later version. It comes with no
warranty. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

It is built with:

- [SDL 3](https://libsdl.org), zlib licence (`packaging/licenses/SDL3.txt`), shipped beside the
  game in the packages;
- [Nuked OPL3](https://github.com/nukeykt/Nuked-OPL3) 1.8 by Nuke.YKT, LGPL 2.1 or later
  (`third_party/nuked-opl3/LICENSE`), the YMF262 emulator the AdLib plays on, with one change,
  marked in its source: the chip keeps each channel's share of its output, for the mixer;
- [Modern DOS 8x8](third_party/modern-dos/README.md) by Jayvee Enaguas, CC0 1.0, from which the
  8x8 font of the DOS prompt was made.

D/Generation was written by Robert Cook and published by Mindscape in 1991; the game, its
files and its text belong to their rights holders. This port is an independent project, not
connected with them, and contains none of the game: it reads a copy the player owns.

# lem_port

**lem_port** brings the 1991 DOS release of *Lemmings* to modern systems –
natively, without an emulator.

It is not a remake and not a reinterpretation. The aim is to play the
original game exactly as it was: the same 120 levels, the same rules and the
same timing, so that every solution that worked in 1991 still works today.

## Why another engine?

The best-known faithful recreation of DOS Lemmings is
[Lemmix](https://github.com/ericlangedijk/Lemmix) by Eric Langedijk – a
remarkable piece of work that captures the original down to its quirks.
Lemmix, however, is written in Delphi and runs only on Windows.

lem_port follows the same path with the same goal of accuracy, written in
portable C++20 on top of SDL3, so the game can be enjoyed on:

* **Linux**
* **macOS**
* **iOS and iPadOS**
* and later in the **browser** (WebAssembly) and on **Windows**

The engine core is free of platform code; each platform only provides a thin
layer for the window, input and sound.

## Game data

The original game files are **not** included and never will be. You need
your own copy of the DOS version of *Lemmings*. Point lem_port at the folder
that contains `main.dat`, `level000.dat`, `vgagr0.dat` and the other data
files – upper or lower case names both work.

## Building

You need CMake 3.20 or newer, a C++20 compiler and, for the game itself,
SDL3.

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build
```

### macOS app to share

```sh
tools/mac_package.sh build-mac
```

builds a self-contained universal `Lem_Port.app` (Apple Silicon and Intel,
macOS 11 or newer, SDL3 built in) and packs it as `build-mac/Lem_Port-macos.zip`.
The app is signed ad hoc; on another Mac open it the first time with right
click → Open.

### iOS and iPadOS

Works on iOS 12 and newer (tested on an iPad mini 2 with iOS 12.5). You need
Xcode, an Apple ID added in Xcode → Settings → Accounts (a free one is fine)
and, for installing from the command line, libimobiledevice
(`sudo port install ideviceinstaller` or `brew install ideviceinstaller`).

```sh
# Xcode project; SDL3 is downloaded and built for iOS
cmake -S . -B build-ios -G Xcode -DCMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME=iOS \
      -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64

# signed build for devices (TEAM = your team id, see below)
cmake --build build-ios --config Release --target lem_port -- \
      -sdk iphoneos -allowProvisioningUpdates DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=TEAM

# install on the USB-connected device and copy the game data
tools/ios_install.sh build-ios/Release-iphoneos/Lem_Port.app /path/to/lemmings
```

* The team id is the `OU=` value of your signing certificate:
  `security find-certificate -c "Apple Development" -p | openssl x509 -noout -subject`.
* A device must be registered with the team once: open
  `build-ios/lem_port.xcodeproj` in Xcode, choose the device and press Run.
  Afterwards the build and `ios_install.sh` are enough.
* With a free Apple ID an installed app runs for 7 days; build and install
  again to renew it. Updates keep the game data.
* iOS 12–14 devices need Xcode's support files for that version in
  `Xcode.app/Contents/Developer/Platforms/iPhoneOS.platform/DeviceSupport`.
* On the first start, trust the developer on the device: Settings →
  General → Device Management.
* The game data can also be copied with Finder (device → Files) or the Files
  app into the Lem_Port folder; the game starts once the files are there.

Touch controls: tap = click (tap a lemming to assign the selected skill),
long press = assign preferring walking lemmings (right button), drag the
level to scroll, double tap TIME for fast forward (it then reads FAST),
three-finger tap
ends a level, two-finger tap returns to the menu from the preview and result
screens.

### Tests

The regression tests in `tests/data_tests.cpp` need the original data and run
only when `LEM_DATA` points to it (`LEM_DATA=/path/to/lemmings ctest ...`).
They play the replays in `tests/replays` and check every level against
`tests/golden.txt`.

On macOS with MacPorts, add `-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/local` to the first
command.
If SDL3 is not installed (many Linux distributions do not package it yet),
add `-DLEM_FETCH_SDL=ON` to download and build it.

## Playing

```sh
Lem_Port --data /path/to/lemmings      # remembered for next time
```

On first start without `--data`, a folder picker asks for the data folder.

| Input | Action |
|---|---|
| Left click on a lemming | assign the selected skill |
| Click a panel button, F3–F10, 1–8 | select a skill |
| F1 / F2, − / + | release rate down / up |
| F11, P | pause |
| Double-click nuke, F12 | nuke |
| F, double click on TIME | fast forward |
| M / X | music / sound effects on or off |
| Arrow keys, mouse at screen edge, minimap | scroll |
| Hold right button | prefer walking lemmings when assigning |
| Alt+Enter | fullscreen |
| Esc | end the level |

Main menu: F1 (or click the sign) plays, F2 enters an access code, F4 shows
the controls, F3 cycles
music + effects / effects only / silence, the arrow keys or the rating sign
change the rating, Esc quits. On the level preview screen the arrow keys and
Page Up/Down (on touch screens a swipe) also choose any level. After a successful level the result screen
shows the access code for the next one; the right mouse button returns to the
menu.

## Tools

`lemtool` lets you look inside the original data files:

```sh
lemtool dat    <file.dat> [outprefix]   # list or extract sections
lemtool gfx    <datadir> <outdir>       # graphics sets as PNG sheets
lemtool levels <datadir> <outdir>       # every level record as PNG + summary
lemtool main   <datadir> <outdir>       # sprites, panel, fonts, menu art
lemtool list   <datadir> [outdir]       # the 120 levels in game order (+ PNGs)
lemtool audio  <datadir> <music|sfx> <n> <out.wav> [seconds]
lemtool replay <datadir> <file.lrp>     # play a replay, print the result
lemtool sim    <datadir> <rating> <n> <outdir> [ticks] [every] [script]
                                        # play a level headless, save snapshots
```

## Documentation

* [Roadmap](docs/ROADMAP.md) – the plan and current progress
* [File formats](docs/formats/README.md) – how the original data is stored
* [Game mechanics](docs/mechanics.md) – how the simulation behaves

## Acknowledgements

lem_port stands on the shoulders of others:

* **DMA Design** created *Lemmings*, published by **Psygnosis** in 1991.
  The game and its data remain the property of their copyright holders.
* **Eric Langedijk** wrote [Lemmix](https://github.com/ericlangedijk/Lemmix),
  the inspiration for this project and the yardstick for faithful behaviour.
* **ccexplore** and **namida** refined Lemmix to match the DOS game even more
  closely; **Aaron Kelley** maintains that work as
  [Lemmix Player](https://github.com/AaronKelley/LemmixPlayer).
* **Aaron Giles** wrote [ymfm](https://github.com/aaronsgiles/ymfm)
  (BSD-3-Clause), which emulates the AdLib's FM chip; it is included in
  `third_party/ymfm`.
* **ccexplore**, **rt**, **Mindless** and **Simon** documented the original
  file formats and shared that knowledge with the Lemmings community.

Thank you all. Apart from ymfm, no code from these projects is included here.

## License

Copyright © 2026 Michał Majchrowicz

lem_port is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the
terms of the GNU General Public License as published by the Free Software
Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later
version. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) for details.

The original game data is not part of this project and is not covered by
this license.

# Tony & Friends in Kellogg's Land
Tools to dissect the 1994 DOS game produced by Factor 5 and Rauser Entertainment.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1974959/69663910-8f5baa00-1087-11ea-8fc1-e91e41b23457.png)

## Game files

| Name | Details |
|:-----|:------|
| START.EXE    | main game binary                             |
| SETUP.EXE    | game setup program                           |
| KELLOGG.INI  | sound card setup data (written by SETUP.EXE) |
| PCKELL.DAT   | Assets container file (see list below)       |
| DPMI16BI.OVL | Borland 16-bit DOS Protected Mode Interface  |
| RTM.EXE      | Borland 16-bit DOS Protected Mode Interface  |


## Asset files

These file types are contained in PCKELL.DAT:

| Ext. | Name | Details |
|:----:|:-----|:--------|
| .MAP | Game Map     | grid based level map |
| .ARE | Area         | |
| .BOB | Animated Sprite | data and x86 code to display; somewhat similar to BOB format of Turrican II |
| .PCC | Image        | PCX version 5, encoded, 8 bit per px |
| .ICO | Sprite Set   | indexed image in EGA pixel order (scrambled columns) |
| .TFX | TFMX Music   | |
| .SAM | TFMX Samples | |

### Game Map

The map files contain a grid of cells (ushort). 9 bits are used for tile ID, the rest is used to describe collision shapes.

## Notes

- START.EXE loads itself after loading DPMI16BIT.OVL (is a EXE) and RTM.EXE.
- Game looks for HISCORE.DAT at launch which does not exist (at least not in my copy of the game).

# BRIX, reimagined

**Play it: [rvenning.github.io/brix](https://rvenning.github.io/brix/)**

A modern, touch-friendly web game built on **BRIX 1.00** — Michael Riedel's 1991
public-domain DOS puzzle game — with **all 112 original puzzles reproduced exactly**.

Push blocks sideways, let them fall, and make touching blocks of the same kind blast
away before the clock runs out. Same puzzles, completely modern game.

## What "exactly" means here

- **Levels.** The 112 levels were extracted from the original `LEVELS` file, not retyped.
  Each encodes back to its original 178 bytes, and each loads identically in the
  original executable's *own* level loader. `npm run validate-levels` → `112 / 112 levels match`.
- **Rules.** The original `BRIX.EXE` runs in a small 8086/DOS emulator in
  `tools/brix-oracle/`. Bots played every level in it while every key pass, fall step and
  elevator step was recorded. The modern engine replays those 112 traces — over 230,000
  steps — and must reproduce the original's state after every single one, including the
  original's quirks (latched keys, stale elevator stack counts, duplicate stack matches).
- **Completion.** A solver has found solutions for 69 levels (36 of the 37 without an
  elevator, 33 of the 75 with one). All 69 replay to a clear as timed key presses through
  the modern scheduler, and all 36 elevator-free solutions also clear the emulated
  original when keyed in. Elevator solutions depend on sub-frame timing, so only 5 of 33
  reproduce in the original's jittery real-time loop; their *mechanics* are covered by the
  traces above.

How the original works — with evidence and open questions — is in
[docs/brix-mechanics.md](docs/brix-mechanics.md).

## Features

- The original campaign: the 7-level tree of choices, time limits, retries, five continues,
  cumulative score, hall of fame, and a saved run you can continue later
- Practice mode with every reached problem, stars, best points and best time
- Original artwork drawn in code: every block type has its own glyph as well as its colour
- Particles, screen shake, eased cursor, smooth elevators, bonus tally — with a reduced-motion setting
- Synthesised sound effects and adaptive music, each switchable
- Keyboard (arrows/WASD, Space, R, Esc), mouse and touch (tap to pick up, drag to push)
- Responsive: desktop, tablet and phone; each level's playfield is cropped to fill the screen
- Level editor: originals open read-only; duplicate to edit, undo/redo, test play, JSON import/export
- Installable PWA that works offline

## Getting started

```bash
npm install
npm run dev        # http://localhost:8129
npm test
npm run build
```

See [docs/development.md](docs/development.md) for the oracle, the solver and debug tools.

## Documentation

| Document | Contents |
|---|---|
| [docs/brix-mechanics.md](docs/brix-mechanics.md) | The original rules, marked confirmed / read from code / unknown |
| [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) | Engine, scheduler, rendering and verification layers |
| [docs/level-format.md](docs/level-format.md) | The `brix-level/1` JSON format and its mapping to the original bytes |
| [docs/development.md](docs/development.md) | Commands, deep links, debug overlay, tooling |
| [docs/brix-history.md](docs/brix-history.md) | Where BRIX comes from |
| [docs/legal-notes.md](docs/legal-notes.md) | Public-domain evidence and what is (not) used |

## Deliberate differences from 1991

These change presentation only; see the architecture doc for why none affects a puzzle.

- Blasts freeze the game for 0.76 s instead of 1.47 s (everything freezes either way;
  "Classic blast timing" restores the original).
- The level tree's 10-second choice timer is off by default (a setting turns it on).
- Block colours are not randomly rotated per problem.
- Two-player alternating mode is not implemented.
- A cross-problem state leak in the original (a stale elevator stack count) is not
  reproduced; each problem starts clean.

## Credits

BRIX 1.00 © 1991 Michael Riedel, released into the public domain. This project is not
affiliated with him or with Epic MegaGames, and uses nothing from later BRIX releases.
Fonts: Fredoka and Nunito (SIL Open Font License).

johnsonfarmsus-alien-legacy-alfix-readme.text:
# ALFIX — Alien Legacy mass-driver fixes + autosave

A patch for **Alien Legacy** (Sierra/Ybarra Productions, DOS, v1.01 and v1.10). It does
three things:

1. **Fixes the game's best-known crash.** Once a colony has a mass driver aimed at
   certain destinations, the game dies whenever the clock advances:
   ```
   DOS/4GW Professional error (2001): exception 00h (divide by zero) at 180:001F75F5
   Crash address (unrelocated) = 1:0002E5F5
   ```
   Sierra's README blames "mass drivers on high-gravity worlds"; the real cause is below.
2. **Makes mass drivers actually deliver.** Aimed at most destinations they never
   fire: their "Turns left" counter is loaded from garbage (often tens of thousands,
   sometimes 0). Same root cause. Fixed, they launch 25 ore every 6 turns, the
   interval the game's own data files specify.
3. **Adds an in-game autosave.** Every 200 turns the game silently writes
   `AUTO1.SAV` .. `AUTO5.SAV` (rotating, so the five most recent are kept) using its
   own save routine. They appear in the normal Load Game list. Nothing changes in
   the UI and your own save name is untouched.

**No game files are included here.** You need your own copy of Alien Legacy. The
game has been out of print for decades; the copy this patch was developed against
came from [My Abandonware](https://www.myabandonware.com/game/alien-legacy-21h).
The patcher only modifies an `AL.EXE` you already have, after verifying every byte
it is about to change.

## Two editions

| | mass-driver fixes | autosave |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Standard** (`ALFIX.COM`, or `python3 alfix.py`) | yes | yes |
| **Fixes only** (`python3 alfix.py --no-autosave`) | yes | no |

Running the patcher on an executable that already has the fixes-only edition
upgrades it to standard.

## How to apply

**Inside DOSBox (no other tools needed).** Copy `ALFIX.COM` into the game folder
(next to `AL.EXE`), then from the DOS prompt in that folder run:

```
ALFIX
```

**From a modern OS with Python 3.** Copy `alfix.py` into the game folder and run:

```
python3 alfix.py                 # standard edition
python3 alfix.py --no-autosave   # fixes only
```

Either way the patcher checks every byte it is about to change, refuses to touch a
file that doesn't match, writes a backup first (`AL.BAK` for the DOS version,
`AL.EXE.ORIG` for the Python one), and reports "already patched" if run again.
To undo, rename the backup back to `AL.EXE`.

**Existing saves.** A mass driver that already has a garbage countdown keeps
counting from it even after the executable is patched (it only reloads on its
next launch). Either take the driver offline and back online in-game, or run

```
python3 alfix.py --fix-saves            # (from the game folder; or pass the SAVES dir)
```

which resets every online mass driver with a garbage countdown to the correct
6-turn cycle, keeping the untouched saves in `SAVES/BACKUP/`. `--fix-saves` knows
the v1.01 save layout only (it skips files of any other size); on v1.10 use the
offline/online toggle instead.

**Versions.** Both patchers detect the version by checking every patch site, and
work on either supported build:

| build | `AL.EXE` | original MD5 | standard | fixes only |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1.01 CD | 827,647 bytes | `fb004009cb1dd703a143a5d9775c5b8c` | `a1998a1e69f2454a5959c2bcea5f9dae` | `9644652f2e9c2b64fb04c5b580f7d010` |
| v1.10 CD (`AL_CD_V1.10`, March 1995) | 936,827 bytes | `e6c78d883eb7972bc4c69098cdeff971` | `0542c76f5d0c7d818ce944a3d292c10f` | `4ca4f029fbbe20bfb4ece0f1bccfd3fc` |

If your `AL.EXE` differs (another release or a floppy version) the patcher will
say so and change nothing; please open an issue with your file's size and MD5.

## What the bug actually is

The per-turn colony cost routine (LE object 1, function at `0x2E469`) walks each
colony's 16 installation slots (27 bytes each, starting at colony offset `0x16E`).
For every active installation it charges an upkeep cost from `INST.DAT`
(52-byte rows), and, if the slot's *product* field (a dword at slot offset 5) is
4 or greater, a second cost taken from `PROD.DAT` (14-byte rows: ore, energy,
life support, humans, robots, **turns**, qty). That second cost is computed as
`value * 24 / turns`.

`PROD.DAT` has 15 rows, so valid product codes are 4..18. The code checks
`product < 4` and skips, but never checks the upper bound:

```
mov  edx, [eax+0x173]      ; product field
cmp  edx, 4
jl   skip                  ; only a lower bound
lea  eax, [edx-4]
imul edx, eax, 14          ; row offset into PROD.DAT
...
mov  ax, [row+10]          ; "turns"
...
idiv ebp                   ; <-- crashes when "turns" is 0
```

For a **mass driver** (installation kind 51, the last row of `INST.DAT`) the same
field doesn't hold a product at all: it holds the **destination colony index**
(33 = SSZeus, 35 = SSCronus, 38 = SSPoseidon in a typical game). Those values
index far past the 15-row table into unrelated memory. Whether the "turns" word
it lands on is zero depends on what happens to be there, which is why some
mass drivers are fine and others crash the game every time the clock advances.
(A side effect: unpatched, mass drivers are charged a nonsense per-turn cost
read from that unrelated memory.)

The same mistake appears in the routine that (re)loads an installation's
countdown (`0x2E070`). Installations with no product take their cycle length from
their own `INST.DAT` row (the word at +0x32); anything with a product code of 4 or
more takes it from the `PROD.DAT` row. A mass driver's destination number sends it
down the second path, so its countdown is loaded from memory past the table:
18,998 turns for one destination, 0 for another. The correct value is right there
in `INST.DAT`: the mass driver's row says **6**. The game's delivery code itself is
fine (it has an explicit mass-driver branch that ships 25 ore to the destination
colony when the countdown expires); it just never gets a sane countdown. Two
other routines on this path (`0x3182C`, `0x327CA`) *do* bounds-check the product
code, so the original programmers guarded most of these lookups and missed two.

## What the patch changes

Bug fixes: five in-place edits, same length as the original code, so nothing else
moves. Autosave: the 6-byte hook, the 152-byte cave and the 4-byte header edit
described above. Offsets are relative to LE object 1; add `0x3E324` for the file offset (v1.01; v1.10 is below).

| obj1 offset | original | patched | effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x2E5B7` | `83FA04 7C3F 8D42FC 6BD00E` | `83EA04 83FA0F 733C 6BD20E` | `cmp edx,4 / jl / lea eax,[edx-4] / imul edx,eax,14` becomes `sub edx,4 / cmp edx,15 / jae skip / imul edx,edx,14`: an unsigned compare rejects codes below 4 **and** above 18, so the table can no longer be over-read. This is the actual fix. |
| `0x2E594` | `89442434 8B6C2434` | `89C5 85ED 740D 9090` | Replaces a redundant register spill with `mov ebp,eax / test ebp,ebp / jz skip`: a zero divisor on the first `idiv` contributes nothing instead of trapping. |
| `0x2E5E8` | `89442434 8B6C2434` | `89C5 85ED 740D 9090` | Same guard on the second `idiv` (the crash site). |
| `0x2A89C` | `31FF 668BB83E950000 89D0 C1FA1F F7FF 89C2` | `0FB7B83E950000 92 99 85FF 7501 47 F7FF 89C2` | A second function (installation cost display) has the same unchecked lookup. Rewritten with `movzx`/`xchg`/`cdq` to make room for `test edi,edi / jnz / inc edi`, so a zero divisor is treated as 1. |

| `0x2E0A1` | `83FE04 7D18 8D04AD00000000 29E8 C1E002 01E8 668B8482D68A0000 EB16 8D46FC 890424 8B3424 C1E003 29F0 668B84423E950000` | `8D46FC 83F80E 7711 89C6 C1E003 29F0 668B84423E950000 EB1A 8D04AD00000000 29E8 C1E002 01E8 668B8482D68A0000 90909090` | The countdown loader's branch selector, rewritten (51 bytes, 4 spare) so that `(product-4)` is compared unsigned against 14: codes 4..18 use `PROD.DAT` as before, everything else (including mass-driver destinations) uses the installation's own `INST.DAT` cycle. Mass drivers now fire every 6 turns. |

For every valid product code the patched code behaves identically to the original.

### v1.10

Sierra's v1.10 release (March 1995) did not fix any of this: its release notes don't
mention mass drivers, and the code still has the same unchecked lookups and unguarded
divisions. The code moved (LE object 1 now starts at file offset `0x45054`) and two
sites are compiled with different registers, so they are re-encoded. Same fixes,
same lengths:

| obj1 offset | v1.01 equivalent | original | patched |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x1C8F7` | `0x2E5B7` | `83FA04 7C40 8D42FC 6BC00E` | `83EA04 83FA0F 733D 6BC20E` (`imul eax,edx,14`: v1.10 keeps the row offset in `eax`) |
| `0x1C8D4` | `0x2E594` | `89442434 8B6C2434` | `89C5 85ED 740D 9090` (identical) |
| `0x1C929` | `0x2E5E8` | `89442434 8B6C2434` | `89C5 85ED 740D 9090` (identical) |
| `0x18B0A` | `0x2A89C` | `31FF 668BB83E950000 89D0 C1FA1F F7FF` | `0FB7B83E950000 92 99 85FF 7501 47 F7FF` (the first 16 bytes of the v1.01 edit; the instruction after it differs in v1.10 and is left alone) |
| `0x1C3E6` | `0x2E0A1` | `83FD04 7D0D 6BC334 668B8406D68A0000 EB1A 8D45FC 890424 8B2C24 8D04C500000000 29E8 668B84463E950000` | `8D45FC 83F80E 7715 89C5 8D04C500000000 29E8 668B84463E950000 EB0F 6BC334 668B8406D68A0000 90909090` (44 bytes; v1.10 holds the product in `ebp` and the kind in `ebx`) |

The other three divisions in v1.10's cost routine are safe, as in v1.01: one is reached
only for product code 4 exactly, one only for installation kinds 0x16/0x19/0x1A, and
one already checks for zero.

The autosave edits for v1.10 are listed in the next section.

## How the autosave works

The game's turn-tick method (`0x41448`, slot `+0x18` of its file-manager object)
ends in a 6-byte epilogue at `0x41523`. That epilogue is replaced by a jump into a
152-byte routine placed in the unused zero padding at the end of the code object
(`0x58D80`; see `autosave.asm`). The routine reads the turn counter; if it is a
multiple of 200 and hasn't been handled yet, it sets the game's save-name global
to `AUTOn` (n = `(turn/200 - 1) mod 5 + 1`), calls the game's own save routine
(`0x40DF0`, which takes no arguments and writes the state plus a copy of
`campaign.tmp`), restores the player's save name, and then runs the displaced
epilogue. It costs a few instructions on ticks that aren't a 200th turn.

The game is relocated at load time, so the routine is position-independent: it
finds its own address with `call/pop` and takes the addresses of the turn counter
and the name string from two existing, already-relocated instructions
(`0x41458` and `0x40E07`). One 4-byte edit to the LE header raises object 1's
declared size from `0x58D68` to `0x59000` so the cave's page is fully mapped.

Tested by driving the game under DOSBox from a turn-4487 save: `AUTO3` was written
at turn 4600, `AUTO4` at 4800, `AUTO5` at 5000 and `AUTO1` at 5200, each a normal
213,605-byte save that loads from the Load Game screen.

### v1.10

v1.10 has the same file-manager object, compiled the same way, so the cave code is
unchanged apart from its addresses (`nasm -f bin -DV110 autosave.asm`). The method
table is filled in at `0x2F6F0`: the save routine is slot `+0x08`, the turn-tick
method slot `+0x18`.

| | v1.01 | v1.10 |
|---|---|---|
| save routine | `0x40DF0` | `0x2F8D0` |
| save-name address (imm32) | `0x40E08` | `0x2F8E8` (`mov esi,save_name`; obj2 `0x39A84`) |
| turn-tick method | `0x41448` | `0x2FF50` |
| turn-counter address (imm32) | `0x4145A` | `0x2FF62` (`mov edx,[turn]`; obj2 `0x35F50`) |
| hooked epilogue `5D5F5E595BC3` | `0x41523` | `0x3002B`, becomes `E960A70300 90` |
| code cave (152 bytes) | `0x58D80` | `0x6A790` |
| LE header, object 1 size | file `0x28780`: `0x58D68` → `0x59000` | file `0x29168`: `0x6A788` → `0x6B000` |

As in v1.01, no fixup touches the 6-byte epilogue or the cave, and nothing else in
the game references the 16 bytes after the save-name string that the routine saves
and restores.

Tested on v1.10 under DOSBox from a new game with a manual save `TEST` at turn 2:
`AUTO1` was written at turn 200 and `AUTO2` at turn 400 (the turn counter is the
dword at offset 1 of a save), each a normal 215,765-byte save that loads from the
Load Game screen, and the player's save name was still `TEST` afterwards.

## Not an emulator problem

This was first suspected to be a DOSBox-X dynamic-core issue on Apple Silicon.
It isn't: the crash reproduces on the interpreter core, DOSBox exits cleanly
(no host crash), and the fault is the game's own `idiv` with a zero divisor.

## Building ALFIX.COM

```
nasm -f bin alfix.asm -o ALFIX.COM
```

`alfix.asm` is plain 8086 code using only DOS INT 21h calls; the resulting
`ALFIX.COM` is about 2 KB. MD5 of the included build: `9191148c04bcc50455fae89814ec8dfd`.
The autosave routine is built separately with `nasm -f bin autosave.asm -o autosave.bin`
(add `-DV110` for v1.10); its bytes are embedded in both patchers.

## Campaign guide

`guide.py` builds a browsable campaign guide from your own game files: all 60
technologies with their effect, the seven science levels each needs, research cost,
the prerequisites the game enforces, the factory or power-plant level each upgrade
unlocks, and the in-game lab reports and encyclopedia text; the technologies the story
depends on; and when each of the 27 cinematics plays. Like the patcher, it ships no
game content; the page is made locally.

```
python3 guide.py                          # from the game folder; writes guide.html
python3 guide.py GAME_DIR OUT.html
```

The story and cinematic sections are written from an analysis of the game's event
scripts. Each `RESOURCE.0xx` file is a small compiled module (32-byte `MZ` header, then
32-bit code) that the game calls with a table of about 150 callback functions; one of
them schedules `?:cinema.NNN`. Films 4, 6, 10, 21 and 27 aren't played by any event.

`TECH.DAT` and `TECHTXT.DAT` are byte-identical in v1.01 and v1.10, so the page is the
same for both.

Formats, as decoded:

- `TECHTXT.DAT` (and the other `*TXT.DAT` files): `u16` string count, `u16` 4, then
  count+1 `u32` offsets (the last marks the end), then NUL-terminated strings.
- `TECH.DAT`: 96 records of 25 bytes, 60 in use. Byte 0 is the kind (2 upgrade,
  4 component or theory, 3 story device, 1 the missile technology); bytes 2–8 are the
  science levels; bytes 9–11 are up to three prerequisite record numbers (`0x63` = none);
  byte 12 is the research cost; bytes 13–24 are six `u16` indexes into `TECHTXT.DAT`:
  effect line, "still needed" message, progress report, completion report, first
  encyclopedia entry, encyclopedia entry.

Two things are inferred rather than stored. Technology names aren't kept as text in
the game files, so each comes from the opening of its encyclopedia entry. The science
order (Astronomy, Geology, Electronics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, Physics) is
read off which level each technology leans on: the plague and the mushroom synthesizer
on Biology, the Translation Constant on Mathematics, the black-hole and orbital devices
on Astronomy.

Alien Legacy itself is © 1994 Sierra On-Line / Ybarra Productions and is not

# Telemark

A ski jumping game for the browser. Its jump physics is a faithful port of Deluxe Ski Jump 2 (v2.10P, DOS, 2001),
reconstructed from an analysis of the original executable and checked against the original game frame by frame.
Graphics, interface and sound are new, made in the style of the original.

![A jumper in flight over the built-in practice hill in snowfall](docs/screenshot.png)

Telemark is a working title.

## Status

As of 2026-10-22: in active development.

- Playable: training mode on 23 built-in hills (K50 to K300) and on the 37 original hills, a replay of the last jump
  (pause, half and quarter speed), the original's `.rpl` replays from your own copy of the game, and competitions
  of two rounds against up to eight computer jumpers with the original's levels and steering (or, as an option, the
  same jumpers landing later and falling less often): one hill, or a World Cup over several hills (also the
  original's double cup) with cup points, standings and a podium.
- A competition is kept on the device between visits and can be saved to a file and read on another device.
- Not there yet: team competitions.
- Playable at <https://telemark.visvaya.workers.dev> since 2026-10-13. The page can be installed and works
  offline after the first visit; every change on the default branch is published there once its checks pass
  (`docs/deployment.md`). Checked by hand on one iPhone and in one desktop browser; not yet on Android.
- Every published change of the game gets a version number, shown in the game and listed under the
  repository's releases.

## Features

- Jump physics, wind, landing and judges' notes identical to DSJ2 v2.10P (deterministic on every device).
- 23 built-in hills, from K50 to ski flying hills of K300; the 37 hills of the original become available when you load `Dsj.exe` from your own copy
  of the game. The file is read in the browser and kept only there; nothing from the original is distributed.
- Mouse, keyboard and touch controls; on phones tilt steering by default, with the finger as the fallback and the
  choice; haptics where supported.
- Pixel graphics with a responsive width, time of day (day, dusk, night) and weather (snow, fog).
- Synthesised sound (Web Audio, no recordings).
- A replay of the last jump, with pause, slow motion and a slider under the picture to any moment; the original's `.rpl` replays play the same way, on
  the hills of your `Dsj.exe`. The replay of each hill record is kept on its own, other jumps by hand or as the
  last few, with an optional clean-up by age and by size; replays go to a file and come back from one, to move them
  to another device (one file, or a ZIP archive with a file for each), and are stored compactly (presses as runs,
  mouse motion only where the jump reacts to it); replays read from files have a group of their own. A replay shows the time of day and the
  weather its jump had. The export of a jump to a `.rpl` file of the original game is written but not offered
  for now: some jumps are still refused although the format could hold them.
- A ghost of the hill record: the record's jump runs beside each training jump, leaving the gate with you.
- Hill records, outfit colours and settings saved locally.
- Installable on a phone's home screen; after the first visit it starts and plays without a network.

## Development

Requirements: Node 26.12.1 or newer, pnpm 12.

```sh
pnpm install
pnpm dev            # development server
pnpm typecheck
pnpm lint
pnpm format         # rewrite the sources in the project's format (oxfmt)
pnpm check:unused   # unused files, exports and dependencies (knip)
pnpm check:duplicates  # duplicated code (jscpd); src/sim is exempt, the port repeats where the original does
pnpm test
pnpm test:coverage  # the tests with the coverage floor for src/sim, as in CI
pnpm test:browser:edge  # the built game in Microsoft Edge on desktop and phone profiles (Playwright)
pnpm test:browser   # the same in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, as in CI; needs Playwright's browsers
pnpm test:scripts   # tests of the build, release and deployment scripts
pnpm build          # production build in dist/, with the service worker and the release record
pnpm check:dist     # dist/ holds exactly the build's files, within the size budgets
node scripts/check-doc-links.mjs  # relative links and backticked repository paths in the Markdown files exist
node scripts/serve-dist.mjs  # the build at http://127.0.0.1:4317, served the way the host serves it
pnpm build:single   # the build packed into one HTML file, in dist-single/
```

Tests that compare the port with the original game need its files and recorded traces; without them they are
skipped. See `docs/testing.md`.

## Repository layout

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `src/sim` | the port of the original physics and jump logic |
| `src/original` | readers for the player's original files |
| `src/game`, `src/render`, `src/audio`, `src/ui` | game session, pixel renderer, sound, React screens |
| `src/storage` | local saves |
| `src/pwa` | service worker registration, offline state, the picture the icons are made of |
| `public` | web manifest, icons, the host's headers file |
| `tools/re` | reverse-engineering tools (disassembler, headless DOS emulator, trace capture) |
| `tools/font` | generators of the screens' font (from the jump picture's own glyphs) and of the Polish letters for the Silkscreen font |
| `scripts` | the release step and service worker, checks of the build and of a deployment, the test server, the single-file build |
| `deploy` | the pinned deployment tool and its configuration |
| `docs` | specifications and guides, see below |

## Documentation

The notes in `docs` are in English.

| File | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| `docs/physics-spec.md` | How does the original move the jumper on the inrun, in flight and on landing? |
| `docs/hill-format.md` | Where does the original keep its hills and how are they read? |
| `docs/hills.md` | How are the game's own hills described, which rules must they pass, and how are they generated? |
| `docs/jump-scene.md` | How does the original draw the jump scene, and where does the port differ? |
| `docs/jumper-figure.md` | How is the jumper drawn from a pose? |
| `docs/replay-format.md` | How are the original `.rpl` replays encoded? |
| `docs/testing.md` | Which tests exist, what do they need and how are they run? |
| `docs/deployment.md` | What is in a release, how does the game work offline and update, how is it deployed and rolled back? |

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome; how to report a bug, propose a change and open a pull request is described in
[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). `master` changes only through pull requests merged by squash, and the pull
request title (Conventional Commits) becomes the commit. CI runs the checks listed under "Development", plus
`pnpm format:check`, a dependency audit, a secret scan, an audit of its own workflows (actionlint, zizmor) and a
check for em dashes and emoji; on `master` the same run can then publish the package it has just tested
(`docs/deployment.md`). `git blame` skips the commit that formatted the whole tree after
`git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs` (GitHub does so by itself). Security reports: see
`SECURITY.md`.

## Credits

Telemark follows Deluxe Ski Jump 2 (v2.10P for DOS, 2001), made by Jussi Koskela (Mediamond), with photographs
by Kalevi Koskela; the Polish translation of v2.10P is by Piotr "V-car" Wikarek. Its jump physics is ported from
that game. Without Deluxe Ski Jump this game would not exist: thank you.

Telemark is made by Maciej Budzyński.

## Legal

This is an independent project, not affiliated with the authors or publishers of Deluxe Ski Jump.
Deluxe Ski Jump is a name of its respective owner and is used here only to describe compatibility. The repository
contains no files from the original game; the game reads them from the player's own copy, locally.

The pixel font is Silkscreen with added Polish letters, under the SIL Open Font License 1.1 (`src/ui/fonts/OFL.txt`;
the built game carries the same text as `licenses/silkscreen-ofl.txt`). The screens' headings and choices use the
jump picture's own font, generated from `src/render/pixel-font.ts` by `tools/font/make_screen_font.py` and licensed
with the rest of the game.

## License

This program is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms of the GNU General Public
License as published by the Free Software Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any
later version. It is distributed without any warranty. See `LICENSE` for the full text.

The license covers this project's own code and documentation. It does not cover the original game, and the font
keeps its own license (see Legal).

# POP-CORN — a measured directory

A byte-level documentation of one installed MS-DOS game directory: nine files,
169,530 bytes, LACRAL software, France, **© 1988**, public domain by its own
statement. **No product bytes are in this repository** — hashes, formats,
figures and the commands that reproduce them are.

## The short sheet

| | |
| --- | --- |
| object | `POP-CORN`, a Breakout game, LACRAL software, MS-DOS, CGA |
| year | **1988**, stated on the manual's own first line |
| authors | **LACAZE Christophe** (code) and **RAYNAL Frédérick** (graphics), named on the manual's first page and again inside the program |
| medium | **none.** A directory on a hard disc, for the third object running — and the first with **no archive either** |
| files | 9, 169,530 bytes, 9 distinct sha1 |
| denominator | **one, D1 = 169,530.** No container, so no second — decided explicitly, chapter 01 |
| coverage | **D1 13.0927 %**, the lowest in the series, and **exactly the ceiling**: 86.9073 % of the object is executable and the rule counts an executable as unidentified |
| third parties | **Microsoft EXEPACK**, inside `popcorn.exe` — 376 bytes of stub, error string and relocation table |
| the packing question | four indicators said packed, eight signature searches said no. **The searches looked for the packer's name, which appears in no packed file.** `RB` at `entry − 2` and `Packed file is corrupt` are what is actually there |
| unpacked | 103,336 → **133,296 bytes**, residue **+0 at both ends** of the decompression |
| the hidden message | **2,418 bytes**, CP437 XORed with 0xAA, inside the packed image. Names both authors, says who did what, and says the graphics were drawn with **NEO on an Atari ST** |
| `.PPC` | `LACRAL` + 49 × 176, residue 0 on 2 of 2. An **8-byte header** and a **12 × 14** grid; three header fields agree with the grid on **98 of 98** blocks |
| levels | 49 in the shipped file, **50 inside the program** — and the hidden message says fifty |
| `.HSC` | a high-score table, 10 × 18 ASCII. **The same extension is AdLib tracker music elsewhere in this collection** |
| sound | one PC-speaker engine, seven tables, **131 bytes and 59 notes**. A game named after a pop tune that never plays it |
| provenance | **one mtime on nine files**, `1996-12-24 23:32:00` — exactly one hour after the thirty-two files of `pc-linksthechallengeofgolf-doc`. Two readings, chapter 10 |
| personal data | **the names yes, the contact details no.** The criterion gained a clause this session — chapter 09 |
| predictions | 60 clauses written first; inherited **9.775 of 13**, open **24.50 of 47** |
| tools | 436 → **443**; seven written, `account.py` rewritten |

## The clause this repository adds to the criterion

The pipeline's fifty-three-session rule — *a name put by its owner inside a
product they made and sold to the public is published* — had never been asked
about a street address belonging to two named private individuals. **The clause
it was missing, in full, with its corollaries and the case that generated it,
is [docs/09](docs/09-the-names.md):**

> **Identity and reach are not the same datum.** A datum that *identifies* a
> person is admitted by the criterion. A datum by which a stranger could
> *arrive at* a person is not, however plainly the product printed it and
> however long ago. Contact details are reported as a shape — kind, count and
> location — and never as their digits.
>
> Because **"published" is not one act.** Publication inside a product is
> bounded by that product's distribution; the same string in a public
> repository in 2026 is indexed, permanent and joined by search to every other
> occurrence of the same name. **Republishing is not repeating.**

## The chapters

| | |
| --- | --- |
| [00](docs/00-predictions.md) | predictions — 60 clauses, written before anything was opened |
| [01](docs/01-the-object.md) | the object — nine files, one denominator, and 13.0927 % said without apology |
| [02](docs/02-the-technical-sheet.md) | the technical sheet — every figure with the command that remakes it |
| [03](docs/03-the-manual.md) | the manual — a construction set, a gift, and three files that are not on the list |
| [04](docs/04-the-packed-program.md) | the program — four indicators, eight failed searches, and a two-byte signature |
| [05](docs/05-the-hidden-message.md) | the message — 2,418 bytes that no `strings` pass could ever have found |
| [06](docs/06-the-levels.md) | the levels — a grid that is twelve wide, and the fiftieth board |
| [07](docs/07-the-user-state.md) | the user state — 180 bytes, three letters, and a number passed in an interrupt vector |
| [08](docs/08-the-sound.md) | the sound — one engine, 131 bytes, and the tune that is not there |
| [09](docs/09-the-names.md) | the names — the clause the criterion was missing, and the door it stops at |
| [10](docs/10-against-the-collection.md) | against the collection — zero over seven roots, one hour, and a checklist that is now due |
| [11](docs/11-the-tools.md) | the tools — seven written, one rewritten, and a self-skip that skipped nothing |
| [12](docs/12-corrections.md) | corrections — nine, of which four are the pre-briefing's and three are this session's own |
| [13](docs/13-leftovers.md) | leftovers — what is still closed, and how close each one is |
| [14](docs/14-prediction-scoring.md) | prediction scoring — 9.775 of 13 inherited, 24.50 of 47 open |

## The tools

`tools/` holds 443 Python files, standard library only, carried forward across
the collection. The seven written here:

    dosimage.py   the four packing indicators for a real-mode MZ image, in one
                  table, with the constant-byte blocks separated from the
                  repeats and a stated minimum block count
    exepack.py    identify, validate and unpack a Microsoft EXEPACK image, and
                  account for every byte of its tail
    popmsg.py     extract the XOR-0xAA credits message; redacts by default
    ppc.py        read a POP-CORN level set to residue zero
    hsc.py        read POP-CORN's high-score table
    pcspk.py      read a PC-speaker note table and render it to WAV
    cga.py        render a byte region as CGA 320x200 — and it identified
                  nothing here, which is chapter 13

Every one of them was made to refuse a specimen that must fail before it was
allowed to census anything.

## What is not here

The nine files of the object. `game/`, `_pre/`, `_work/` and `prompt.txt` are
in `.gitignore`, verified in both directions with `git check-ignore` and with
`git add -An` before anything was committed. The object's own prose is quoted
only where a measurement needs it, and its authors' contact details are not
quoted at all.

# pc-bianconatale-doc

A measured description of one directory: eighteen files, 1,436,520 bytes,
holding **BIANCO NATALE** — a Christmas platform game by Tecnoart Software
Development, Genova, MS-DOS, VGA mode 13h, Italian, 1994. The object is not
published here. What is published is what could be counted, decoded, rendered
and checked.

## The short card

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **what it is** | a four-level platform game: you are Father Christmas, the wizard Magoon has brought your furniture to life, and you throw snowballs at it — and roughly a sixth to a third of the object is the studio advertising itself and an encyclopedia |
| **studio** | Tecnoart Software Development, Genova |
| **year** | 1994 — a DOS timestamp inside a modern ZIP, plus the string `Bianco Natale (1994)`: two independent things, not thirteen |
| **platform** | MS-DOS, VGA (mode 13h), mouse, Turbo-C, not packed |
| **files** | 18, one flat directory, 0 subdirectories |
| **bytes** | 1,436,520 |
| **distinct sha1** | 18 — nothing repeats |
| **mtime waves** | 8 over 13 days on the 1994 clock, ending on the build |
| **coverage** | specified 4.8838 %, derived 95.1162 %, **opaque 0.0000 %**, residue 0 |
| **the pictures** | two undocumented formats, 94.4746 %, closing on their own length; 16 files and 129 animation frames, **rendered and looked at for the first time** |
| **crossings** | 0 of 18 hashes over 111 repositories |
| **tools** | 586 Python files: 582 inherited (2 repaired), 4 written |

**The lowest opening coverage this collection has measured — 4.8838 %.** One MZ
header was the entire identified content of the object when the session began.
The other 95 % is raw eight-bit pixels behind five- and seven-byte headers whose
arithmetic had closed at residue zero before the session started — and had
closed on a header **four bytes too long**, which is the first thing this
session found ([docs/03](docs/03-two-picture-formats.md)).

**What this object has that no object here has had:** no documentation at all.
No manual, no licence, no readme, no order form, no paper credits. The only
prose is a data segment inside `BN.EXE` — the plot, the menu, an advertisement
for an encyclopedia, and the names its own linker forgot to hide
([docs/06](docs/06-the-program.md)).

**What was opened:** both picture formats and the font, from the bytes; the
sixteen pictures, rendered and described — a snowman title, Magoon's castle, a
sprite bestiary of walking gift-boxes and pumpkin ghouls, an encyclopedia
mock-up ([docs/04](docs/04-what-the-pictures-show.md)). **What was not:**
`BN.EXE`'s code, and therefore the exact layout of the four levels — the
decision and its argument are in [docs/06](docs/06-the-program.md) and
[docs/11](docs/11-not-measured.md).

## The chapters

Eleven, and the count is the object's, not a convention. The three objects
before this ran nine, ten and twelve chapters; here the pictures are 94 % of the
object and take two — the formats, and what they depict — because a residue-zero
closure is a necessary condition for reading a picture and not a sufficient one,
and the difference between the two is a chapter. The clocks take one because
yesterday they were worth an hour and here they are worth eight.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| [01 — BIANCO NATALE: the only prose is inside the program](docs/01-what-this-is.md) | what it is, the denominator, and why a 4.8838 % opening figure is not "unreadable" |
| [02 — The technical sheet](docs/02-the-technical-sheet.md) | every figure with the command that makes it again |
| [03 — Two picture formats](docs/03-two-picture-formats.md) | the header that was four bytes too long, and the trailer that was a screen position |
| [04 — What the pictures show](docs/04-what-the-pictures-show.md) | rendered for the first time: a snowman, a castle, and a sprite bestiary |
| [05 — The font](docs/05-the-font.md) | ten lines that turn an arithmetic into a letter, and tell ink from outline |
| [06 — The program](docs/06-the-program.md) | one unpacked Turbo-C binary, and 334 symbols the linker left behind |
| [07 — Five menu entries, two not the game](docs/07-the-menu-and-the-advert.md) | how much of a Christmas game is an advertisement, and whose route PCDISK is not |
| [08 — Three clocks](docs/08-three-clocks.md) | the 1994 clock, the repackager's, and the one unzip wrote this afternoon |
| [09 — The box](docs/09-the-box.md) | four tools written, and one defect class repaired for the third object running |
| [10 — Corrections and calibration](docs/10-corrections-and-calibration.md) | three figures re-counted, six guesses scored three and three, +5.00 |
| [11 — What is not measured](docs/11-not-measured.md) | the levels, the third trailer word, and what is outside this folder |

## The rules this repository works under

* **Nothing is executed, installed or emulated.** Rendering a `.BMB` reads
  bytes out of a data file with a grammar derived from those same bytes; no
  instruction from the object is run. The object arrived as a ZIP and was
  extracted, which is none of the three — but extraction wrote eighteen mtimes
  that are not the object's, so the wave table is built on the 1994 DOS field
  and the mtimes are thrown away ([docs/08](docs/08-three-clocks.md)).
* **Every figure names its denominator**, and every figure has a command in
  [docs/02](docs/02-the-technical-sheet.md) that reproduces it.
* **A file name is not a measurement.** `TITLE.BMB` was a name until a snowman
  came out of it; the "what it is" of every picture is this session's reading of
  the pixels ([docs/04](docs/04-what-the-pictures-show.md)).
* **Files are selected by grammar, never by extension.** `bmb.py` refuses
  `BN.EXE` and the font; `fnt.py` refuses the pictures.
* **A residue-zero closure is necessary, not sufficient.** Both formats closed
  on a header this session then had to move by four and six bytes
  ([docs/03](docs/03-two-picture-formats.md)).
* **There is no witness, and none was invented.** The run of three
  owner-witnesses ended with this object; it speaks for itself, out of its own
  data segment ([docs/01](docs/01-what-this-is.md)).

## The tools

`tools/` holds 586 Python files and is published whole. Four were written here —
`bmb.py`, `fnt.py`, `zipclocks.py`, `menushare.py` — and each has a `--selftest`
that passes in a repository that does not contain this object, or says how many
checks it skipped and why. Two inherited tools were repaired: `symtab.py`, whose
capitals-only pattern saw 20 symbols of 334 and whose repair uncovered a second
defect that had inflated a neighbour's published count by five
([docs/09](docs/09-the-box.md)); and `coverage.py`, given a length channel so a
64,777-byte picture can be recognised from a 4,096-byte head.

```
python tools/bmb.py       --selftest      44 checks, 0 failures, 0 skipped
python tools/fnt.py       --selftest      30 checks, 0 failures, 0 skipped
python tools/zipclocks.py --selftest      21 checks, 0 failures, 0 skipped
python tools/menushare.py --selftest      11 checks, 0 failures
```

# roth_ripper
An archive extractor tool for the DOS game Realms of the Haunting (1996).

There is an older version of this tool floating on the internet; I advise to forget about it and refer to this one instead,
since the older version had some bugs that got addressed here (e.g. DBASE300/208.tga had the wrong colors, and DBASE300.DAT wasn't extracted properly
if it belonged to a game version without .midi files, to name a few) and this is a bit more polished in general.</br>
There's probably more polishing/refactoring that needs to be done, but for now I'd say it can stay as it is.

## Usage
Create a directory and place the following files in it:

- roth_ripper.exe
- ICONS.ALL
- BACKDROP.RAW
- FXSCRIPT.SFX
- DBASE200.DAT
- DBASE300.DAT
- DBASE500.DAT
- ADEMO.DAS
- DEMO.DAS
- DEMO1.DAS
- DEMO2.DAS
- DEMO3.DAS
- DEMO4.DAS

Then simply launch the exe and a "ROTH_Resources" subdirectory should be created in the same directory where you've put all the files, which is going to contain all the extracted material.

If you're taking files from the game's CD, I'd suggest to take DATA/FX22.SFX and rename it to FXSCRIPT.SFX instead of taking DATA/FXSCRIPT.SFX;
they contain the same sounds, but some sounds in DATA/FX22.SFX are 22050 Hz while the sounds in DATA/FXSCRIPT.SFX are all 11025 Hz (lower quality).

## Extracted material
- Videos (.gdv files from DBASE300.DAT; go [here](https://www.realmsofthehaunting.com/downloads.html) to get a DOS .gdv player)
- Textures
- Sprites
- Various graphics (menus, HUDs, icons, etc)
- Palettes
- Sounds (including the speech audio files from DBASE500.DAT)
- Music

All picture-related material is extracted as .TGA pictures, which can be viewed fine with
IrfanView (albeit without transparency), SLADE3, MtPaint, and possibly other image viewers I'm unaware of;
if that's still a problem for you, Ken Silverman's PNGOUT is your friend :)

As for music, depending on the game version you're extracting you might have both .HMP files and their .midi counterparts, or just .HMPs;
in the latter case, foobar should play them just fine (see [here](http://www.vgmpf.com/Wiki/index.php?title=HMP) for more info).

# quiver_ripper
An archive extractor tool for the DOS game Quiver (1997).

Apologies for the less than optimal code: this tool was done a while ago and was among my first ripper programs. Nonetheless, considering it serves its purpose just fine and is more or less comprehensible as it is, I don't think a rewrite is necessary.

## Usage
	quiver_ripper G.bin
where G.bin is the game's archive name passed as an argument(in Windows you can also use the drag-and-drop method).
Once the extractor has done its thing, you should have the extracted resources in a subfolder
located in the same path as the archive (if you didn't use the drag-and-drop method, you should see the subfolder's path
printed as soon as the extraction is done, just in case).

## Extracted material
- Textures
- Sprites
- Various graphics (fonts, menus, HUDs, etc)
- Palette
- Sounds
- Music

All picture-related material is extracted as .TGA pictures, which can be viewed fine with
IrfanView (albeit without transparency), SLADE3, MtPaint, and possibly other image viewers I'm unaware of;
if that's still a problem for you, Ken Silverman's PNGOUT is your friend :)

As for sounds and music it's a bit trickier since the game uses Diamondware STK as sound library, with its own custom formats
(.DWD for sounds, .DWM for music), with DWD which appears to be derived from .VOC and .DWM which is MIDI converted into
a custom format which seems to make use of OPL commands; if you're that interested, Dynamo128's packaged resources
(which you can find [here](https://forum.zdoom.org/viewtopic.php?f=37&t=50106)) include PLAYDWD.EXE and PLAYDWM.EXE tools
(part of Diamondware STK library), which work under DOSBox and play those custom formats just fine.

If you want to convert .DWM files back to MIDI, I explained how to do that [here](https://forum.zdoom.org/viewtopic.php?p=949676#p949676).

As for .DWD(sound) files, I might look them up at some point, even though in all honesty they didn't seem they were worth the effort.

That's all, for now :)

# IslandPerilExtractor

IslandPerilExtractor is a tool designed to extract and process resources from `.ipw` files, specifically for the game "Island Peril". It can extract files embedded in the `.ipw` archive and process `.PIC` image files to generate PNG images.

## Features

- Extracts files from `.ipw` archives.
- Processes `.PIC` image files to generate PNG images.
- Supports parallel processing for faster image conversion.
- Handles transparency in `.PIC` images and saves both regular and transparent versions.

## Requirements

- .NET 9.0 or later.
- [SixLabors.ImageSharp](https://github.com/SixLabors/ImageSharp) library for image processing.

## Usage

1. Build the project using .NET 9.0 or later.
2. Either drop the `.ipw` file onto the exe, or run the application with the following command:

   ```bash
   IslandPerilExtractor <ipw file> 
   ```

   - `<ipw file>`: Path to the `.ipw` file to extract.

## Example

```bash
IslandPerilExtractor C:\path\to\file.ipw
```

This will extract the contents of `file.ipw` to `C:\path\to\extracted_resources` and process any `.PIC` files found.

## Output Examples

# Paranoid Level Designer

*An unofficial level editor for Paranoid, the 1993 DOS game.*

**Paranoid** is an Arkanoid-style DOS game from 1993 by Ben and Tom North
("The Bit Bucket Brothers"). This is an unofficial level editor for Paranoid
v1.8. It is a real DOS program that runs next to the game in DOSBox, and it
draws everything with the game's own bricks, icons, fonts and logo.

![The designer, with a level drawn in bricks that reads 2026](screenshots/editor-2026.png)

![The level list: all thirty levels as small pictures](screenshots/level-list.png)

![Icon mode, showing the icons hidden in the bricks, and a marked block](screenshots/icons-and-block.png)

## Features

- Edit all 30 levels: every brick type, and the 12 power-up icons hidden
  inside bricks.
- Works with the keyboard alone or with the mouse:
  - Tab moves between the play area, the brick panel and the level box.
  - Shift+arrows draw as you move.
  - Mark a block to fill, empty or copy it.
- Copy and paste, mirror, clear and undo.
- **Level list (F6):** add a new level anywhere, delete, duplicate and
  reorder levels.
- **Test-play (F5):** runs Paranoid with your level as level 1, and puts
  everything back afterwards, high scores included.
- **Safe saving:** your original levels are kept, and a failed save can't
  damage the game's levels file. See below.
- Help pages and a title screen in the style of the original game.

## Getting started

You need **Paranoid v1.8**, the 1993 shareware release, and
[DOSBox](https://www.dosbox.com/). The game itself is *not* included here.

1. Download `DESIGNER.EXE` from the [Releases](../../releases) page.
2. Copy it into your Paranoid folder, next to `PARANOID.COM`.
3. Start DOSBox in that folder and run the designer, for example:

   ```
   dosbox -c "mount c C:\GAMES\PARANOID" -c "c:" -c "DESIGNER"
   ```

Press **F1** in the designer for help.

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| Arrow keys / Shift+arrow keys | Move / draw while moving |
| Space, Delete | Place / remove the chosen brick or icon |
| Tab, Ctrl+arrow keys | Move between screen areas / choose a brick |
| I | Switch between bricks and icons |
| B | Mark a block (then Space, Delete or C) |
| C, V, M, U, N | Copy, paste, mirror, undo, clear the level |
| PgUp, PgDn | Previous / next level |
| F2, F3 | Save / load (last save, backup or original) |
| F4, F5, F6 | New level / test-play / level list |

## Your original levels are safe

The game has only one levels file, `LEVELS.PAR`, so the designer is careful
with it:

- **`LEVELS.ORG`:** on the first save, the original levels are copied here.
  This file is never written over.
- **`LEVELS.BAK`:** before every save, the previous version is copied here.
- If a backup can't be made, nothing is saved.
- New levels are written to a temporary file first, and replace `LEVELS.PAR`
  only once complete.
- **F3 → Original** brings back the game's own levels.

The game always plays exactly thirty levels. An empty level is passed over as
soon as the ball is launched, so keep your levels at the front of the list.

## Building from source

The designer is one C file, built with
[Open Watcom 2.0](https://github.com/open-watcom/open-watcom-v2) for 16-bit DOS:

```
set WATCOM=C:\WATCOM
BUILD.BAT
```

Don't add `-ox`: its loop optimiser miscompiles the video code.

## Credits and legal

- **Paranoid** © 1993 Ben North and Tom North. This project is not affiliated
  with or endorsed by them.
- No part of the game is included in this repository. The designer reads the
  graphics, fonts and levels from your own copy of Paranoid when it runs.
- The designer's source code is released under the [MIT License](LICENSE).

## Sentinel Worlds I: Future Magic save game editor
Version: 0.8 (Beta)

Author: Kinda Lee Hutchinson but really Claude.ai Code

This editor modifies save game files from the 1989 MS-DOS game "Sentinel Worlds I: Future Magic".

**Implementations available:**
- **macOS Native (Swift/SwiftUI)** - Native macOS application with modern UI
- **Python TUI (Cross-platform)** - Textual-based terminal UI (primary Python interface)
- **Python GUI (Cross-platform, legacy)** - Tkinter GUI for macOS/Linux/Windows
- **Python CLI (Cross-platform, legacy)** - Text menu interface

All versions can modify:
- Party cash and light energy
- Individual character stats, abilities, and inventory
- Ship software levels
- Crew member portraits (8 character faces)

---

## macOS Native Version (Swift/SwiftUI)

**Requirements:** macOS 13.0 (Ventura) or later

The native macOS application provides a modern SwiftUI interface with full feature parity to the Python version.

**Building from source:**
```bash
# Open the Xcode project
open SentinelWorldsEditor/SentinelWorldsEditor.xcodeproj

# Build and run in Xcode (Cmd+R)
# Or build from command line:
xcodebuild -project SentinelWorldsEditor/SentinelWorldsEditor.xcodeproj \
           -scheme SentinelWorldsEditor \
           -configuration Release
```

**Features:**
- Native macOS performance and look-and-feel
- Tree-based navigation with master-detail layout
- Real-time validation with visual feedback
- Full undo/redo support (Cmd+Z / Cmd+Shift+Z)
- Unsaved changes warnings
- Equipment selection via dropdown menus
- Keyboard shortcuts (Cmd+O, Cmd+S, Cmd+W, Cmd+Q)
- 37 unit tests for binary I/O and data validation

The compiled app can be found in Xcode's DerivedData folder after building.

---

## Python Version (Cross-Platform)

**Requirements:** Python 3.10 or later, plus `textual` (installed automatically via pip)

The Python version provides a Textual-based terminal UI (TUI) as its primary interface, with legacy CLI and Tkinter GUI interfaces also available.

### Installation

**Option 1: Install with pip (Recommended)**
```bash
# From the project directory
pip install .

# Or install directly from your Git repository
pip install git+https://github.com/code-a-saurus/SWEditor.git
```

After installation, you can run any version from anywhere:
```bash
# Terminal UI (primary interface — keyboard-driven, works in any terminal)
sw-editor-tui

# Graphical interface (window-based, legacy)
sw-editor-gui

# Command-line interface (text-based menu, legacy)
sw-editor path/to/gamea.fm
```

**Option 2: Run directly from source**
```bash
# Terminal UI
python3 src/tui.py

# Graphical interface
python3 src/gui.py

# Command-line interface
python3 src/main.py path/to/gamea.fm
```

### Python Usage

You need to provide your own Sentinel Worlds I save game files (gameX.fm where X = A-Z).

#### Terminal UI (Recommended)

Launch the TUI for a keyboard-driven full-screen interface that works in any terminal:
```bash
sw-editor-tui
# or if running from source:
python3 src/tui.py
```

**TUI Features:**
- Full-screen terminal interface built with Textual
- Keyboard-driven navigation (no mouse required, mouse supported)
- Tree-based navigation of all save game elements
- Inline editing with validation
- Equipment selection via dropdown menus
- Unsaved changes tracking
- Automatic backup creation before any changes

#### Legacy Interfaces

The Tkinter GUI (`sw-editor-gui`) and text-menu CLI (`sw-editor path/to/gamea.fm`) remain
available but are no longer the primary supported interfaces.

### Python Uninstallation

If you installed the Python version with pip:
```bash
pip uninstall sentinel-worlds-editor
```

---

## License

Both the Swift and Python implementations are licensed under the GNU General Public License v3.0 or later. See the LICENSE file for details.

Tools for the MS-DOS version of Turrican II, written in C# for .NET

File formats reverse-engineered 
by [movAX13h](https://github.com/movAX13h/) and [srtuss](https://github.com/srtuss), July 2018. 

![Sprites of Turrican II](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/movAX13h/turrican2tools/master/screenshots/sprites.png)

## Features

 - load/unpack original game data
 - view/play/export files
 - [custom TFMX player by srtuss](https://github.com/movAX13h/turrican2tools/tree/master/TFXTool)
 - save sprites and tilesets as PNG
 - modify all files (hex editor)
 - repack game data

## TODO

 - map entities to IDs (the boring stuff)
 
## EIFS - Executable Integrated File System

All data of the game is packed and appended to the main game executable in form of EIFS blocks. The last EIFS block is read first by the game and contains a TOC for all other files.

### Identification
6 bytes at end of file/section:
```
2 bytes ... length of section
4 bytes ... signature "EIFS"
```

### Unpacker

Turrican II stores its asset files as an obfuscated, or compressed and obfuscate stream of bytes.
The stream may be split into sequential compressed blocks that must be decompressed individually, each giving a portion of the unpacked file.
Every asset file uses a block-size of 1024 bytes (that means that every compressed block produces 1024 unpacked bytes), with exception of the TOC file, which is treated as a single block, and may exceed that limit.

Every compressed block starts with a word N, which states the length of the block, followed by N bytes of data.

The first byte of this data selects wether LZ compression is used.

If LZ is used, the stream is a series of instructions, with respective payload:

 - **move**: decipher a byte from the input stream, and write it to the output buffer
 - **repeat**: repeat a string that was decompressed before, by performing a string-copy within the output buffer
 - **fill**: decipher the given byte, and write it to the output buffer a given number of times

If LZ is not used, the data is an uncompressed block of ciphered bytes.

Turrican II uses an XOR cipher of 0x6B. For details see 
[AssetLoader.cs](https://github.com/movAX13h/turrican2tools/blob/master/T2Tools/Turrican/AssetLoader.cs)


### Table Of Contents (TOC)

Consists of a list of 24-byte entries. The list has a fixed maximum size, holding space for 300 entries (7200 bytes). Empty entries are filled with 00.
```
12 byte ... filename, maximum 12 characters, padded with whitespace characters (0x20)
 4 byte ... unpacked file length
 4 byte ... packed stream start position (counted from the beginning of the exe file)
 4 byte ... packed stream end position (counted from the beginning of the exe file)
```
For details see 
[AssetLoader.cs](https://github.com/movAX13h/turrican2tools/blob/master/T2Tools/Turrican/AssetLoader.cs)

## File Types
 
The game uses the following file types:

| Extension | Type(s) | Description | View/Play |
| --------- |:-------:|:----------- |:--:|
| .EXE | Executables | SETUP.EXE, INTRO.EXE, WORLD[1-5].EXE, ENDPART.EXE | |
| .BOB | Sprites | May contain multiple frames of varying size | x |
| .MC  | Sprites | Boss sprites | |
| .PCX | Sprite | UI, intro ground and T2 logo | x |
| .PIC | Tileset | Tilesets per world | x |
| .RAW | Bitmap | CRUSH1.RAW, CRUSH2.RAW | |
| .MAP | Map | Maps for each stage (tilebased grid) | x |
| .PAL | Palette | Colors for all parts of the game | x |
| .COL | Collisions | Tile based collision info per world | x |
| .EIB | Entities | Grid based list of entities for each cell of a stage (IDs are hardcoded in the game) | x |
| .TFX | Music | [TFMX](https://www.exotica.org.uk/wiki/TFMX) songs by Chris Hülsbeck | x |
| .SAM | Sound | raw 8-bit signed mono PCM data, containing every sample, per world | |
| .LNG | Language file | All strings in 4 languages | x |
| .TXT | Text | TEXT2.TXT contains the intro text | x |
| .FNT | Pixelfont | Font | |
| .FON | Font | Textmode font (used by the setup) |
| .DAT | unknown | same extension used for various file types | |
| .DIR | unknown | COMIC.DIR, 224 bytes |
| .P   | unknown | ? |
| .CHG | unknown | W3.CHG, 72 bytes
| .ANI | unknown | LINE.ANI, 1368 bytes
| .DLT | unknown | ANIM2.DLT, 262211 bytes

## Tools used

DOSBox Debugger, IDAPro, VisualStudio, HEX editors, custom binary visualizers
